Lesson 71 correlated all 31,878 pairs of lesson 63’s 253 rules over the twenty-eight moves on which every rule in the grid is defined. The median pair came to 0.9472 and 8.93 per cent of the pairs were the same series to the last decimal.

Lesson 74 measured the same 31,878 pairs on each half of that window separately. Over the first fourteen moves the median is 0.8871 and 9.50 per cent of pairs are identical. Over the last fourteen the median is exactly 1.0000 and 72.23 per cent are identical.

A trader runs several rules whose average pairwise correlation is 0.9247, which is what lesson 74 measured on the worse of its two fortnights. Lesson 67 needed 589 trades to settle whether an edge of a tenth of an R was real, and lesson 65 fixed the pace at forty trades a month.

Six positions, each risking 1.5 per cent of the account, at lesson 71’s measured correlation of 0.9472. The variance of a sum of N positions of equal size is the single-position variance multiplied by N times one plus N minus one times r.

Lesson 72 evaluated the one-factor integral for the day on which every position goes against you: at six positions it is 0.3838 at this correlation and 0.0156 if the six were independent. Take a month as 21 trading days, and take lesson 18’s median worst drawdown of 9R.

Lesson 73 forbade the short and the optimiser put everything into two of the four rules. Here are those two, with the standard deviations and the correlation lesson 71 measured over the same twenty-eight moves: the 2-and-5 rule at 0.6375, the 8-and-30 rule at 0.7032, and a correlation between them of 0.6282.

Lesson 74 measured the four rules’ average pairwise correlation three ways: 0.5673 over the first fourteen moves, 0.7887 over all twenty-eight, and 0.9247 over the last fourteen. The instrument’s own standard deviation over the second fortnight is 1.195 times its standard deviation over the first.

The standard correction for that bias divides the measured correlation by the square root of one plus delta times one minus the correlation squared, where delta is the ratio of variances minus one. The book is four positions at two per cent each in every case, and the all-against frequencies are 0.2222 at the lowest correlation and 0.3868 at the highest.

What does the correction do to the 0.9247? What are the bets and the day’s standard deviation at each of the three correlations? And how much more often does the all-against day arrive on the second fortnight than on the first?

Take lesson 74’s worst-window correlation of 0.9247, at which the all-against day arrives on 38.68 per cent of days for four positions. Compare the permitted book against a single position carrying the same four per cent of heat, which loses its whole heat whenever it loses at all.
The counts are one multiplication each. 0.0893 × 31,878 = 2,847 over the full window, 0.0950 × 31,878 = 3,029 over the first fourteen moves, and 0.7223 × 31,878 = 23,027 over the last fourteen.

The ceiling is one division. The bets a book carries are N over one plus N minus one times r, and as N grows without limit that goes to one over r. At 0.9472 the ceiling is 1.0558, at 0.8871 it is 1.1273, and at exactly one it is exactly one.

Read the third window twice. A median of 1.0000 does not mean the rules are similar. It means more than half of the pairs in the grid produced the same fourteen numbers as each other, so the ceiling is not approached from below, it is reached: no number of rules from that family, run over that fortnight, carries more than one bet. And the middle window holds fewer identical pairs than the first even though it contains the fortnight in which almost everything tied, because agreeing on twenty-eight numbers is harder than agreeing on fourteen.
2,847, 3,029 and 23,027 identical pairs, against ceilings of 1.0558, 1.1273 and exactly 1.

The limit is one over 0.9247, which is 1.0814, and the wait it leaves is 0.9247 of the original: 0.9247 × 589 is 544.6 trades and 13.62 months. There is no number of rules at this correlation that gets the wait below thirteen and a half months, because the limit does not contain N at all.

And six independent rules would have needed 589 ÷ 6 = 98.2 trades each, which is 2.45 months. The distance between 2.45 and 13.80 is the whole of what the word diversification is usually carrying, and it is bought with a number nobody measures.
1.0391, 1.0599, 1.0670 and 1.0814 bets; 567, 556, 552 and 545 trades; 14.17, 13.89, 13.80 and 13.62 months; a correlation of 0.2000 for three bets; and 2.45 months if they were independent.

The summary is the standard deviation. One plus five times 0.9472 is 5.7360, six times that is 34.4160, its square root is 5.8665, and at 1.5 per cent a position that is 8.80 per cent. So the day sits 96.2 per cent of the way from the 3.67 per cent six independent positions would give to the 9.0 per cent that arrives when the six move as one.

The frequencies are one multiplication each. 0.3838 × 21 = 8.06 days a month, against 0.0156 × 21 = 0.33, which is one such day every three months. The ratio is 0.3838 ÷ 0.0156 = 24.6, and it is bought with no change to any position size, any stop or any rule.
9.0 per cent of heat, a day of 8.80 per cent, 8.06 all-against days a month against 0.33, a ratio of 24.6, and 9R in 3.9 trading days.
The covariance is 0.6282 × 0.6375 × 0.7032 = 0.28162. The two variances are 0.40641 and 0.49449.

The weight on the 2-and-5 rule is (0.49449 − 0.28162) ÷ (0.40641 + 0.49449 − 2 × 0.28162) = 0.21287 ÷ 0.33766 = 0.6304, so the other weight is 0.3696. Those are the 0.630 and 0.370 on the card, arrived at from two standard deviations and one correlation rather than from a matrix inversion.

The variance they deliver is 0.6304² × 0.40641 + 0.3696² × 0.49449 + 2 × 0.6304 × 0.3696 × 0.28162 = 0.36029, whose square root is 0.60024. Equal weights give 0.60501, so the whole prize on this pair is 0.79 per cent of the day.

The short is a comparison rather than a calculation. The weight on the second rule is its own variance minus the covariance, so it turns negative when the covariance exceeds the first rule’s variance, which is when r exceeds 0.6375 ÷ 0.7032 = 0.9066. Below that the optimiser holds both. Above it, it wants to sell the noisier rule to hedge the quieter one, and the correlations lesson 74 measured on its worse fortnight sit above it.
0.6304 and 0.3696, delivering 0.60024 against 0.60501 equally weighted, a cut of 0.79 per cent; and the short arrives above a correlation of 0.9066.
Delta is 1.195² − 1 = 0.4280. One minus 0.9247² is 0.1449, so the denominator is the square root of 1 + 0.4280 × 0.1449 = 1.06202, which is 1.03055, and 0.9247 ÷ 1.03055 = 0.8973.
That is a real correction and it does not rescue the measurement: 0.8973 still sits far above the first fortnight’s 0.5673, so the volatility explains part of the move and not most of it.

And the frequency is one division: 0.3868 ÷ 0.2222 = 1.74. The same four positions, sized identically, hand you a day on which everything goes against you three quarters again as often, and nothing about the book changed. Only the fortnight the correlation was measured in did.
The 0.9247 corrects to 0.8973; the bets are 1.4804, 1.1883 and 1.0599 and the days 6.58, 7.34 and 7.77 per cent; and the all-against day arrives 1.74 times more often.

The single position at four per cent has a day of 4.00 per cent and pays its whole heat whenever it loses, which is half the time. Four positions at one per cent give 1 + 3 × 0.9247 = 3.7741, four times that is 15.0964, and the square root is 3.8854, so the day is 3.89 per cent and the whole heat arrives 38.68 per cent of the time.

So the day is (4.00 − 3.89) ÷ 4.00 = 2.86 per cent smaller and the full-heat day is (0.5000 − 0.3868) ÷ 0.5000 = 22.6 per cent rarer. That is the entire benefit of running four rules rather than one, after five lessons of measurement, and it costs a quartering of the size per trade to collect. Independent, the same swap would have given a day 50 per cent smaller and a full-heat day 87.5 per cent rarer.

Four positions, a day of 3.89 per cent against 4.00, which is 2.86 per cent smaller, and a full-heat day 22.6 per cent rarer; and the card deletes 5-and-20 and zeroes 3-and-10 as well.

Module 10 leaves the arithmetic and starts on the day, and finds the day is not short of hours but short of decisions: of the 253 rules on the grid, 138 produce exactly one entry over the stretch they are defined on, and the busiest cell in the whole grid works out at seventy-five entries a year.
